paras.text: The Standard Fire Policy, M C L Five Hundred Point Two Eight Three Three, Audio Lecture
This is the backbone statute of Michigan property insurance, and I want to tell you up front why it repays the effort more than almost anything else in this track.

Every fire policy sold in this state, and every homeowners policy built on top of a fire chassis, has to contain a specific list of provisions. That list lives in one section: M C L five hundred point two eight three three. So when you are standing in an argument about a claim, you are almost always arguing about a lettered subdivision of one statute. Know it cold and you can point to the exact letter of the exact subsection that controls.

The hard part of this chapter is that it is a list of letters, a through s, and a pile of numbers. A list is the easiest thing in the world to nod along to and the hardest thing to keep. So I am going to teach it in groups that belong together, and I am going to teach the numbers in pairs, because the wrong answer is almost always the other number in the pair.
Thirteen ideas. After most of them, a question and then silence. Answer out loud.
Idea one. Where this statute came from, and one honest gap.

Section two eight three three sits in Chapter twenty eight of the Insurance Code of nineteen fifty six, the chapter called Fire Insurance Contracts, which runs from section two eight zero four to section two eight six six.
The section itself was added in nineteen ninety, by Public Act three oh five, with immediate effect on December fourteenth of that year.

It replaced an older approach, and the history matters because it still has legal force. Until the end of nineteen ninety one, Michigan had a separate section, five hundred point two eight three two, that spelled out an actual standard fire policy form, word for word. The same nineteen ninety act repealed it, effective January first, nineteen ninety two. Today the legislature's website shows only a one line compiler's note saying it, quote, pertained to form of standard policy, end quote.

So here is an honest gap, and I would rather hand you the gap than a confident guess. I cannot tell you word for word what that old form said, because its text was not verified against a primary source.

What is certain is this. The modern statute, in subsection two, still leans on that repealed section as a floor. Every fire policy must contain, at minimum, the coverage that was in the standard fire policy under former section two eight three two. The old form is gone as a document, but its substance survives as an incorporated minimum.
Hold the pair: two eight three three is the live statute, two eight three two is the repealed form that still sets the floor underneath it.
Idea two. Letters a and b. What must be covered at all.

Subsection one is the list, lettered a through s, of provisions every fire policy issued or delivered in Michigan must contain. This is the state's non negotiable checklist, no matter which company writes the policy.

Letter a is the actual cash value floor. The policy has to cover, at minimum, the actual cash value of the property at the time of the loss. A carrier can offer more, replacement cost coverage for example, but it can never offer less than actual cash value as the baseline. Floor, not ceiling. That phrase is going to come back three more times in this chapter.

Letter b is the core peril, plus a rule people forget exists. Minimum coverage is direct loss by fire and lightning. And on top of that, pro rata coverage for five days for property that gets moved to another location to save it from a covered peril.

Picture what that is actually for. Furniture carried out of a burning house, sitting in the yard, and then it rains on it for two days. That five day removal provision is what protects it. It is a small rule that shows up on real jobs constantly.
Question. What is the minimum a Michigan fire policy must pay on the valuation side, and how long does removed property stay covered.
Actual cash value at the time of the loss, under letter a, and five days of pro rata coverage for removed property, under letter b.
Idea three. Letters c through g. The disclosure block.
These five hang together, so learn them as a block rather than five separate facts. They are all about the policy telling you where coverage stops.
Letter c lets the policy be void for misrepresentation, fraud, or concealment.
Letter d requires the policy to state what property is not covered.
Letter e requires it to state what perils are not covered.
Letter f requires a statement of what conditions suspend or restrict coverage.
And letter g requires a provision for waiving or changing a policy term.

Notice the theme. The statute is not deciding what gets excluded. It is requiring that the exclusions be written down where you can find them. Property, perils, conditions, and how terms change. That is the block.
Idea four. Letters h and i. Cancellation, taught as a pair.
These two are mirror images, and the exam of real life will hand you one and see if you apply the other one's rule.

Letter h is the insured's right to cancel. The insured can cancel at any time. The insurer's minimum earned premium is not less than the pro rata premium for the expired time, or twenty five dollars, whichever is greater.

Do the arithmetic on that, because that is where it becomes real. Somebody cancels early in the term and the pro rata number works out to eight or nine dollars. The insurer still keeps twenty five, because twenty five is greater. Whichever is greater always favors the insurer here.

Letter i is the mirror image, the insurer's right to cancel. The insurer can cancel at any time too, but it has to mail written notice to each named insured, at their last known address, at least ten days before cancellation takes effect, postage fully prepaid.

The same twenty five dollar or pro rata minimum earned premium applies. And if there is excess premium the insurer is not tendering up front, the cancellation notice itself has to say that the excess will be refunded on demand.
So the pair is: either side may cancel at any time, the same twenty five dollar floor applies to both, and only the insurer owes the ten day mailed notice.
Question. Insurer cancels. How much notice, delivered how, and what happens to leftover premium it is not sending along with the notice.

At least ten days, mailed written notice to each named insured at the last known address, postage fully prepaid. If it is not tendering the excess premium, the notice has to state that the excess will be refunded on demand.
Idea five. Letter j. The mortgagee clause.
This one matters because almost every damaged house has a mortgage, and this is where a lot of real money gets stuck.
If loss is payable to a mortgagee who is not named as an insured, the insurer can cancel that mortgagee's interest by giving the mortgagee at least ten days written notice.

Now here is the piece people forget, and it is the one that saves claims. If the insured never gets around to filing proof of loss, the mortgagee itself, once notified, has sixty days to render its own proof of loss.

Hear the pair inside a single letter: ten days to cancel the mortgagee's interest, sixty days for the mortgagee to file its own proof of loss. Ten and sixty, both in letter j, doing completely different jobs.

Two more mechanics. If the insurer pays the mortgagee while denying the underlying claim against the homeowner, the insurer steps into the mortgagee's shoes for recovery, which is subrogation, up to the amount it paid, without cutting off the mortgagee's own right to sue. Alternatively the insurer can pay off the mortgage debt entirely and take an assignment of the debt and the mortgage. Either side, or both together, can sue to recover their respective shares.
Idea six. Letters k and l. Two short ones.
Letter k is the pro rata other insurance rule. If a second policy also covers the same peril, the first insurer's liability is capped at its pro rata share, not the whole loss.
Letter l simply requires the policy to state its notification requirements when a loss occurs.
Idea seven. Letter m. Appraisal, and the numbers to carve in.
This is probably the single most tested provision in the whole section, so slow down here.
If the insured and the insurer cannot agree on the actual cash value or the amount of the loss, either party can make a written demand for appraisal.
Once that demand goes out, each side has twenty days to pick its own competent, independent appraiser and name that appraiser to the other side.

The two appraisers then have to agree on an umpire. If they cannot agree within fifteen days, either side can ask a circuit court judge, in the county where the loss happened or where the property sits, to pick the umpire for them.

The appraisers set the amount item by item. If they agree, that is the number. If they do not, they kick their disagreement to the umpire, and a written agreement signed by any two of the three, meaning the two appraisers, or one appraiser plus the umpire, sets the final amount of loss.
On cost: each party pays for its own appraiser, and the umpire's fee and the other appraisal expenses split fifty fifty.

Say the numbers back with me. Twenty days to name an appraiser. Fifteen days to agree on an umpire. Any two of three sign off. Twenty and fifteen, in that order, and the order is the thing people reverse.

Now memorize the limit of what appraisal actually does, because this is where the real fights happen. The statute's own words limit it to the amount of the loss or the actual cash value. Whether something is covered at all is a coverage question.

The Court of Appeals held in Maksym versus Auto Owners, a published twenty twenty six decision, that an insured is not entitled to appraisal on items whose coverage is still in dispute. That dispute goes to court, not to the appraisal panel.

Question. Carrier agrees the water damage is covered but says your number is too high, and separately says the hardwood floors are not covered at all. Which part goes to appraisal, which part does not, and what are the two clocks.

The amount dispute goes to appraisal. The coverage dispute over the floors does not, under Maksym. Twenty days to name your appraiser, fifteen days for the appraisers to agree on an umpire before either side can ask a circuit court judge to pick one.
Idea eight. Letters n and o. The insurer's options, and no walking away.
Letter n gives the insurer options besides paying cash. It can repair, replace, rebuild, or simply take the damaged property.
That is a real right, not a formality. When a carrier sends a letter saying we are sending our own crew, that is letter n. It is rarely used, and it is genuinely theirs.

Letter o shuts the door on abandonment. There is no right for the insured to just hand over the wreckage and expect a full payout as though it were a total loss without going through the claim process.
So the pair: the insurer may elect to take the property, and the insured may not force it on them.
Idea nine. Letter p. The payment clock, and its exception.
The loss is payable within thirty days after the insurer receives proof of the amount of loss.
But notice the opening words of the letter, because they matter more than people think: except as otherwise provided in section two eight four five.

Section two eight four five is Michigan's municipal escrow withholding statute, which we will get to in a moment. Where it applies, part of the payment can be legitimately delayed and redirected under its own separate rules.

So here is the practical consequence. A payment that runs past thirty days because of a two eight four five escrow is not a violation of the thirty day rule. If you accuse a carrier of blowing the clock when an escrow is in play, you will be wrong, and you will have spent your credibility.
Idea ten. Letters q, r, and s. The suit clock and two closers.
Letter q is the suit limitation clause, and it has a built in trap.
An action under the policy must be commenced within one year after the loss, or within whatever longer period the policy itself specifies.
Here is the twist. That clock is tolled, meaning paused, from the moment the insured notifies the insurer of the loss until the insurer formally denies liability.

So an insured does not always have exactly one year from the date of loss to sue. Work the example. The insured notifies the carrier promptly, and the carrier takes a year and a half to formally deny the claim. The suit clock has been sitting paused that entire time. It only starts ticking again once that formal denial happens.
If you had counted a flat year from the date of loss, you would have told that homeowner she was out of time when she was not.
Letter r requires the standard subrogation provision: the insurer steps into the insured's shoes to recover from any other party responsible for the loss.
And letter s sets the effective time for every fire policy under this section: twelve zero one a m, standard time, at the location of the property.

Subsection two, as I said at the start, ties the whole thing back to that repealed former section two eight three two, requiring the minimum coverage of that old standard fire policy as a floor, on top of everything in subsection one.
Question. Loss on May first, reported May first, formal denial fourteen months later. Is the homeowner out of time, and why.
No. The one year clock under letter q was tolled from notice until formal denial, so it was not running during those fourteen months. It starts at the formal denial.
Idea eleven. The two escrow statutes, and why they get confused.

These two sections, five hundred point two eight four five and five hundred point two two two seven, are constantly mixed up, so let me separate them by the one thing that actually divides them: the size of the community.

Both let a municipality require an insurer to withhold twenty five percent of a fire loss settlement, as security to make sure a damaged structure actually gets fixed or torn down instead of left standing as a hazard. Twenty five percent is common ground.

Section two eight four five covers the smaller municipalities. Cities, villages, and townships in counties under four hundred twenty five thousand people, as long as that particular city, village, or township does not itself have fifty thousand or more residents. Its residential cap has been twelve thousand dollars since two thousand fifteen, adjusted every January first by the consumer price index.

Section two two two seven is the mirror statute for the bigger jurisdictions. Counties of four hundred twenty five thousand or more, plus any city, village, or township of fifty thousand or more even inside a smaller county. And two two two seven also covers a wider range of perils. Not just fire and explosion, but vandalism, malicious mischief, wind, hail, riot, and civil commotion.

Now the critical twenty twenty four update, and this is where most stale material goes wrong. Public Act eighty two of twenty twenty four amended section two two two seven, and only two two two seven, raising its residential cap from twelve thousand dollars to twenty four thousand dollars, effective July first, twenty twenty four, and switching its adjustment date to every July first instead of January first.
Section two eight four five was not touched. It is still on the old twelve thousand dollar, January first schedule.
So the two statutes now run on different numbers and different calendars. Twelve thousand on January for the small municipalities, twenty four thousand on July for the big ones.

Which brings us to the current bulletin. D I F S Bulletin twenty twenty six dash sixteen dash I N S, issued and entered June second, twenty twenty six, and signed by Director Anita G Fox, sets the section two two two seven maximum withholding amount at twenty five thousand ninety dollars, effective July first, twenty twenty six, through June thirtieth, twenty twenty seven. This bulletin supersedes the prior year's bulletin. And for context, the year before that, July first twenty twenty five through June thirtieth twenty twenty six, the figure was twenty four thousand ninety six dollars.

Twenty five thousand ninety dollars, and it belongs to section two two two seven, not two eight four five. If you attach that number to the wrong statute you have made exactly the mistake this idea exists to prevent.
Question. A fire in a township of eight thousand people, in a county of two hundred thousand. Which escrow statute, which cap, and which adjustment date.

Section two eight four five, because the county is under four hundred twenty five thousand and the township is under fifty thousand. Twelve thousand dollar residential cap, adjusted every January first. The twenty five thousand ninety dollar figure belongs to two two two seven and does not apply here.
Idea twelve. The escrow rhythm both statutes share.
Once you know which statute applies, the sequence is the same, and it is a clean chain of numbers.
The municipality gets fifteen days after the withholding notice to say it wants the money escrowed, or the funds default to the insured.
Once escrowed, the insured has ten days to object.
If a mortgage is in default, the treasurer releases funds to the first mortgagee within ten days of a written request.

If nobody shows reasonable proof of repair or demolition within one hundred twenty days, the municipality can use the retained money itself to secure, repair, or demolish the structure, returning any leftover to the insured.
And an insured who wants to sue a municipality to get withheld proceeds back has three years from the original withholding notice.

There is also an opt out, and it is the most useful thing in this idea for somebody in the trades. File a qualifying repair contract with the insurer within fifteen days of the final settlement, consent to paying the contractor directly, and have the insurer notify the municipality, and there is no withholding at all.
Fifteen, ten, ten, one hundred twenty, three years. And fifteen again for the opt out.
Idea thirteen. How this maps onto a real policy and a real job.
A modern H O three policy is built on the same fire coverage base this statute governs, and its Section One Conditions roughly track two eight three three's subdivisions.

A condition called Appraisal mirrors letter m's twenty day and fifteen day mechanics. Our Option mirrors letter n's repair, replace, rebuild, or take language. The Mortgage Clause mirrors letter j. And Suit Against Us mirrors letter q.

One careful point on that last one. Some policies give two years to sue, and in Michigan that longer period controls, because letter q says one year or the policy's period, whichever is longer. The statute is a floor, not a ceiling. A policy may lengthen the suit window. It can never shorten it below one year, and it can never drop the tolling.
Now the job site version, which is where this stops being academic.
Letter j's mortgagee mechanics matter because loss checks are so often made out jointly to the homeowner and the bank, and a slow homeowner can trigger that separate sixty day mortgagee clock.

Letter m's appraisal right belongs to the insured, not the contractor. And here is the line to be careful about. A contractor whose detailed estimate supports the homeowner's own appraisal demand is doing legitimate work. A contractor who personally demands appraisal or negotiates the umpire for a fee is edging into unlicensed public adjusting under a different statute, five hundred point one two two two. Same job site, two very different sides of a licensing line.
Letter n's insurer option clause is why a we are sending our own crew letter from a carrier is a right the statute actually gives them, even if it is rarely used.
Letter p's thirty day payment clock is the number a contractor plans draws and cash flow against.
And letter q's one year, tolled suit clock matters because a contractor's timeline and lien strategy have to be planned against the homeowner's outer legal deadline.
Time for the rapid fire recap. Fast, as a self check.

Twenty five dollars or pro rata, whichever is greater, for either party's cancellation. Ten days mailed notice for an insurer cancellation, and ten days notice to cancel a mortgagee's interest, with sixty days for a mortgagee to render its own proof of loss. Twenty days to name an appraiser, fifteen days to agree on an umpire, any two of three sign the amount. Thirty days to pay after proof of amount of loss, subject to section two eight four five. One year to sue, or the policy's longer period, tolled from notice to formal denial. Twelve zero one a m as the effective time. Twenty five percent withholding under both two eight four five and two two two seven, but two eight four five's cap is twelve thousand dollars on a January schedule, while two two two seven's cap is twenty four thousand dollars on a July schedule since Public Act eighty two of twenty twenty four, now twenty five thousand ninety dollars for July twenty twenty six through June twenty twenty seven under Bulletin twenty twenty six dash sixteen dash I N S.
Lock these numbers in. If any of the questions I asked gave you trouble, that is exactly where to drill.
